doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Break for tea; Miss Marple films and Lawrence of Arabia
summary: Tea service chat, then Hendricks talks about Margaret Rutherford films and Robert Bolt's screenplay.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah. We’re going to take a little break here and we’ll get our tea. That’s amazing.

But it was just everyday life to us, that’s just what went on. And actually in a lot of ways it was much more picturesque than it is now because there were no illusions about it. Everybody knew what was happening. Now everything is dressed up under a façade and actually the same thing is happening. The gangsters are functioning and they’re functioning because the politicians are helping them, the judges are helping them, and it’s all hidden beneath some kind of mask. Earl Gray — oh I hate it when they do that, they put the milk in a glass. It’s going to be all over the saucer and the table. Why do they do that? I think I’ll spoon it out. I hate hotel service. Very seldom do they give you service.
They should have the people that make this stuff up sit and do this. So they know the kind of thing they’re giving people to deal with.

Put it in one of those little pitchers you know, so that you could pour it into the — and have a teapot. Well you know tea should be in a pot. The British know how to do this. Look at it already. I lived in London for five years with my family. Boy they do tea. Where are we, 61st?
Yeah, between 61st and 62nd I think we are. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

Where is the Stanhope? It’s Fifth Avenue across from the Metropolitan Museum. What street is that, 81st isn’t it? But anyway they do an English tea that’s outasite. It’s real. I’ll have to clean this up.

Yeah that’s the best way. Because if you try to pour it it’s going to be all over the saucer. I just watched three of the Miss Marple movies with Margaret Rutherford. Did you ever see those things? You should buy those, those are great. They’re made with MGM money that they earned in England, and at that time you couldn’t take it out so they started making movies over there, and they found this Margaret Rutherford woman who had been a Vaudevillian for years, and she was kind of past her prime so they cast her as Miss Marple. Oh man, she’s too much. She is too much, this lady. And they’re well written, and they’re very good stories, and they make a very entertaining movie. So I bought all three of them and I screened them all day yesterday. Really good. And they used the best English actors, like one of them was with Robert Morley, who is a favorite of mine, and another one is with Lionel Jeffries, and another one was Arthur Kennedy who was very good. But Margaret Rutherford, big, wide woman — ugly as homemade sin but funny as hell. I’m also trying to get —
Can we put this over here?

Sure. I’m also trying to get a transcript of the screenplay to “Lawrence of Arabia” by Robert Bolt. Best screenwriting in the history of film. It’s so beautiful, the language. I don’t know how many times you’ve watched that movie.
A couple of times I’ve seen it, yeah.

Watch it again and just listen to the language, don’t pay too much attention to the visuals, which is hard because they’re superb too. But listen to the language, it’s incredible to think a guy wrote this. It’s fantastic. It’s literature of the highest order. Robert Bolt. Boy.
